text: In Book II of the Republic, education begins with stories, because children hear stories before they ever train their bodies (376e–377a). The founders of the city must therefore supervise the story-makers, and Socrates lays down two laws for what may be said about the gods. The first law is that God is good, and for that reason the cause of good things only (379b–c). Nothing good can harm. The evils of the world far outnumber the goods, and some other cause must be found for them. The second law is that God neither changes nor deceives (380d–383a). Whatever is in the best condition is least altered from outside, and a perfect being would never willingly change for the worse. Three kinds of story are thrown out of the city: Homer's two jars at the threshold of Zeus (379d), every poet who blames a god for the ruin of a house, and every shape-shifting god of the old tales. Socrates then turns to lying. The lie that gods and human beings hate most is the one lodged in the soul, which is the state of being deceived about reality in the part of oneself that matters most (382a–b). A lie spoken aloud is hated less. A god has no lie in the soul and no motive to put one in anyone else's.
